absorptionBoosters: Eating a varied diet with whole grains, pulses, nuts, seeds and greens, which lifts total intake
Splitting supplement doses across the day and taking them with food (less stomach upset)
Fermenting whole-grain batters (dosa, idli, sourdough-type) may free soluble magnesium (in-vitro evidence; human absorption data Not found)
Well-absorbed supplement forms such as citrate or glycinate versus oxide (evidence mixed; head-to-head human data weak)
absorptionBlockers: Phytate (whole grains, pulses, nuts) binds magnesium, partly offset by the higher magnesium content of whole foods
Oxalate in spinach and similar greens
Very high doses at one time (fraction absorbed falls and diarrhoea is more likely)
Heavy alcohol use, chronic diarrhoea or vomiting (higher losses)
Loop and thiazide water pills and long-term proton pump inhibitors (higher losses)
Magnesium taken within 2 hours of oral bisphosphonates, or close to tetracycline/quinolone antibiotics (they bind each other)

warnings: General information, not medical advice. Check with a doctor before starting magnesium supplements.
Kidney disease: magnesium supplements, magnesium antacids and magnesium laxatives can cause high blood magnesium. Do not self-start; doctor input needed.
Heart-rhythm medicines, digoxin, diuretics, PPIs, bisphosphonates and tetracycline or quinolone antibiotics interact with magnesium or change magnesium levels; ask a doctor or pharmacist.
The 350 mg/day limit (US) applies to supplements and medicines, not to food. Loose stools or diarrhoea are the usual first sign of too much supplemental magnesium.
Labels may show the salt weight; enter the elemental magnesium figure.
ICMR-NIN requirement values for magnesium were seen only through secondary reports and could not be verified against the NIN document.

conditionAdjustments.change: Kidneys clear magnesium, so supplements, magnesium antacids and laxatives can build up to high blood levels as kidney function falls; food magnesium target is not changed by the app. Requires doctor input; no supplement presets shown.
conditionAdjustments.source: Clinical reviews of magnesium in CKD (PMC9920010, PMC11317063); Mayo Clinic supplement page

conditionAdjustments.change: No change to the food target. Observational data (NHANES 2011-2018) link higher dietary magnesium with lower odds of stones; randomized evidence is limited and routine supplements are not supported over standard therapy. Supplements: doctor first.

No ICMR change found. Pooled cohort studies link each extra 100 mg/day of dietary magnesium with about 14-19% lower diabetes risk (RR 0.81-0.86; observational). Small Indian studies report low serum magnesium in 12-45% of people with diabetes. Metformin or insulin users: doctor first for supplements.
conditionAdjustments.source: Diabetes Care 2011 meta-analysis; PMC5133122; JK Science 2022 and other Indian studies

conditionAdjustments.change: No target change found. Supplements lower BP by about 2-3 mmHg on average (larger in people on BP medicines or with low magnesium); not a replacement for medicines. Diuretic users: loop and thiazide types raise magnesium loss, potassium-sparing types lower it; doctor first.

ICMR value Not found. EFSA sets no extra need (AI 300 mg/day); NIH RDA 350-360 mg/day. App shows the adult-woman ICMR value as a floor; supplement dose is the doctor's decision. Requires doctor input.
ICMR value Not found. NIH RDA 310-320 mg/day; EFSA AI 300 mg/day (no extra). App shows the adult-woman ICMR value. Requires doctor input for supplements.
conditionAdjustments.source: EFSA 2015 and 2017 DRV summary; NIH ODS

conditionAdjustments.profileId: P20 Osteoporosis and low bone density
conditionAdjustments.change: No target change found. Higher dietary magnesium is associated with higher hip bone density in observational data; no strong trial evidence for supplements. Magnesium taken within 2 hours of oral bisphosphonates can reduce their absorption.
conditionAdjustments.source: NIH ODS health professional fact sheet; PubMed 26556742

conditionAdjustments.change: No target change. Proton pump inhibitors taken for 3 months or more (most cases after a year) can cause low magnesium (FDA label warning); magnesium-containing antacids add magnesium. Ask a doctor about checking blood magnesium.
No target change found. Diarrhoea and other gut losses can lower magnesium; magnesium salts are osmotic laxatives and can worsen loose stools. Supplements: doctor first.

conditionAdjustments.profileId: P19 Celiac disease and gluten sensitivity
conditionAdjustments.change: No ICMR change. Harvard Health lists digestive disorders such as celiac disease among causes of higher deficiency risk even with adequate diet. Doctor guidance for testing.

conditionAdjustments.profileId: P21 Heart disease (after a cardiac event)
conditionAdjustments.change: No target change. Both low and high magnesium can affect heart rhythm; Mayo advises telling the doctor about heart disease before magnesium supplements. Heart-rhythm medicines: doctor input needed. Requires doctor input.
ICMR age-60+ value Not found; NIH RDA 420 mg (men) and 320 mg (women) from age 31. Older adults and people on diuretics or PPIs are more likely to run low; kidney function matters before supplements.
No change found in the sources read. Sweat losses of magnesium: Not found.

conditionAdjustments.profileId: P33 Jain diet (no root vegetables; nutrient gaps and swaps)
conditionAdjustments.change: No change found. Nuts, seeds, millets, whole pulses and leafy vegetables remain available; Jain-specific magnesium data Not found.

conditionAdjustments.profileId: P34 Vegan diet (no dairy, eggs, meat, fish or honey)
conditionAdjustments.change: No change found. Plant foods (seeds, nuts, millets, pulses, greens) are the main magnesium sources; vegan-specific magnesium data Not found.
